column2: Soil replacement can be carried out above the groundwater level, and in most cases the fill under the footings is only partly replaced.
What gases can form in made ground?
Only water vapour
Toxic (e.g. cyanide) and explosive (methane) gases
Only oxygen
Helium
It must be expected that toxic gases (e.g. cyanide) and explosive gases (methane) can also form in made ground.
Which is NOT characteristic of organic soil?
Dark colour
Low unit weight
High water content
High oedometer modulus
The modulus of organic soil is small (300–2000 kPa); it is dark, light, has a high water content and is often fibrous.
What is the typical oedometer modulus of organic soil?
Eoed = 300–2000 kPa: an extremely small value.
With a good cover layer, which foundation should be examined first?
A deep pile foundation
A shallow footing, as narrow as possible
A wide raft on the peat
A partial basement
With a cover layer in good condition, the possibility of a shallow foundation should be examined first.
Why is a narrower footing in the cover layer an advantage?
Because the formwork is cheaper
Because the influence depth decreases, and less stress reaches the organic layer
Because the safety against bearing failure is greater
Because the peat consolidates faster
The narrower the footing, the smaller the influence depth, and the less stress reaches the organic layer.
What happens if the groundwater level drops permanently?
The peat swells
The peat dries, shrinks and decomposes: the ground and the building settle
The peat hardens
Fluctuating groundwater is dangerous for organic soils: they shrink considerably when they dry out.
What should be avoided on organic soil?
A compact plan
Three-dimensional stiffening
Partial basements and extensions
Flexible service connections
Partial basements and extensions should be avoided; design a building with a compact plan and three-dimensional stiffening.
Why is the consolidation of organic soil slow?
Because its permeability is high
Because its permeability (k) is low
Because it contains little water
Because its unit weight is high
k is small, so consolidation is slow; in addition, organic decay makes secondary compression last a long time.
A single-storey house near Szolnok: after the dry summer of 2022, cracks rising towards the corners appeared. In spring the cracks almost closed.
Seasonal opening and closing and the drought are the hallmarks of expansive clay.
A house above a row of wine cellars in Mezőföld: it was fine for decades, then after a water pipe leak one of its corners settled 8 cm in a few days.
Sudden, one-off settlement caused by water: collapse in loess.
A gap site in Budapest: pieces of brick and concrete, slag and broken glass come out of the excavation, and there is a faint smell in the basement.
Mixed, man-made material: made ground. The smell may indicate gas formation.
A new housing estate in a river valley: in the borehole, under 1.5 m of sand, there is a black, fibrous, very light layer; its water content is 380%.
Dark, fibrous, light, an enormous water content: peat, that is, organic soil.
Settlement is larger on the side facing the 20 m tall row of poplars next to the house, and diagonal cracks run along the wall facing the trees.
The thirsty tree dries out the high-plasticity clay: shrinkage, uneven settlement.
The floor of a hall built on an area filled 6 years ago without compaction settled in patches after a wet spring.
Fresh, uncompacted fill that collapses when soaked. Fill less than 8–10 years old is very dangerous.
Because of pumping at a nearby gravel-pit lake, the groundwater level dropped by 1.5 m; over a few years the houses and the ground in the area started to settle slowly and unevenly.
Drying organic soil shrinks and decomposes: fluctuating groundwater is dangerous for it.
A plot along a high river bank: the oedometer test with flooding gave iᵣ = 0.035.
iᵣ > 0.01: soil at risk of collapse, probably loess.
If the three conditions of collapse are met, widening the footing protects the building.
It does not: the building cannot be protected from sudden settlement even by increasing the safety against bearing failure.
Damage caused by expansive clay typically appears after a long dry summer.
Especially if several dry years follow one another.
A partial basement is a good compromise on expansive clay.
A partial basement is the worst solution on such ground.
The depth of seasonal movement is about 2–2.5 m.
The foundation level should not be closer than this to the ground surface.
Swelling clay can lift a lightly loaded building.
In wetter weather the swelling clay lifts the lightly loaded building, and the cracks narrow.
On expansive clay it is mainly the superstructure that should be strengthened, not the foundation.
The other way round: the foundation should take the bending and tension, not the superstructure – strengthen the foundation instead.
A poplar near the house is favourable, because its roots stabilise the clay.
The roots of a thirsty tree (poplar, birch) draw the water from under the footings, so the clay shrinks.
On expansive clay the house needs paving 1.0–1.5 m wide around it, sloping away.
This way rainwater does not soak in next to the footings.
When dry, loess can stand in a vertical face.
This is why wine cellars could be dug into it. Soaked, however, it collapses.
Collapse is cyclic: after the water is removed, the soil rises again.
Collapse happens once and is irreversible.
A soil is at risk of collapse if the collapse coefficient exceeds 0.01.
Loose, uncompacted fill less than 8–10 years old can also collapse.
This is why it counts as a collapsible soil.
Wet, saturated loess can collapse under its bare load alone.
Water weakens the calcite and clay bridges holding the grains together, so in saturated loess the load alone can trigger collapse.
On collapsible soil, roof water should be led into a soakaway next to the house.
Roof water must be led away from the building in a closed drain.
Soil burning has been abandoned for environmental reasons.
Heat treatment and soil burning are rarely used today.
The density of made ground is typically uniform.
The density and compressibility of made ground can vary within wide limits.
57% of the damaged partition walls in Hungary stood on fill.
40% of the structural elements, 57% of the partition walls, 70% of the floors.
Most of the damage on made ground is triggered by water.
87% of the damage was triggered by water.
On made ground the contact pressure may safely exceed 300 kPa.
The contact pressure should not exceed 150–200 kPa.
Explosive methane can also form in made ground.
And toxic gases too, such as cyanide.
A plate compactor can compact a layer 2–4 m thick.
A plate compactor 10–30 cm; the 2–4 m refers to the dropped tamping plate.
A dropped tamping plate can compact made ground 2–4 m thick.
Displacement piles also act as stiffening elements.
They compact the ground, and stiffening elements are placed under the structure as well.
Soil replacement can be carried out below the groundwater level without any problem.
Soil replacement can be carried out above the groundwater level.
In made ground, cement grouting should be carried out from the bottom upwards.
Grouting should be done from the top downwards, with a small amount of bentonite.
Crushed concrete can be used as a replacement material.
Sandy gravel, crushed stone, crushed concrete or stabilised transitional or cohesive soil.
Of the organic soils, peat is the most dangerous.
But silts and clays with a higher organic content are also unfavourable.
The water content of organic soil can be several hundred per cent.
w > 50–70%, but it can be several hundred %.
The oedometer modulus of organic soil is high.
On organic soil, consolidation is slow because of the low permeability.
k is small, consolidation is slow.
Organic soil is insensitive to heat.
It is sensitive to heat; warmth dries it out.
With a good cover layer, the footing over the peat should be as wide as possible.
